Captain, yes, we can copy it. TinyKeyboard installs onto your phone without an App Store Connect key, and Talon can use the same route.

**How TinyKeyboard does it** (`~/code/TinyKeyboard/ota-publish.sh`):
1. It builds an ad-hoc-signed `.ipa`.
2. It writes an install page and an install manifest (`itms-services`) next to the `.ipa`.
3. Tailscale serves them over HTTPS on the tailnet.
4. You tap the link in Safari on the phone and the app installs.

No cable, no TestFlight and no App Store Connect key are involved. Your phone just needs to be registered with the signing team.

**What differs for Talon** (`talon-palette-ios`):
- **Team:** Talon is set to team `85PWBA3B59`. TinyKeyboard uses team `TV2582LRYN` and its ad-hoc install works. We either register your phone under the Talon team or switch Talon to the TinyKeyboard team.
- **Pipeline:** Talon is built for TestFlight upload, which is why it's stuck on the key (task-ldkqx). It has no ad-hoc install route yet.
- **HTTPS path:** the install needs an HTTPS address on the tailnet. Talon's feed already runs at `https://macbook.hippo-tilapia.ts.net:7399`. The `.ipa` and manifest would be served from an HTTPS address on that same machine.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Wake the primary firstmate when a new bead lands in the Parlay inbox.
# Tails ~/data/inbox/events.jsonl (one JSON line per created bead, the same
# stream `parlay inbox-tail` consumes) from a persisted byte offset and files
# one idempotent captain-inbox note per bead id via fm-inbox.sh.
# Events with "type":"comment" (new comment on an existing bead) file a note keyed
# parlay-inbox-<id>-c<N> so each new comment count wakes firstmate once.
# The loop reads the batch from fd 3: `inbox show` is an ssh-backed wrapper that
# would otherwise consume the loop's stdin and silently drop the rest of a batch.
set -u
FM_HOME=/Users/trilliumsmith/fm_home/firstmate
EVENTS=${INBOX_EVENTS_FILE:-$HOME/data/inbox/events.jsonl}
STATE=$HOME/.local/share/fm-parlay-inbox-watch
OFF=$STATE/offset
mkdir -p "$STATE"
CHUNK=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$CHUNK"' EXIT
[ -f "$OFF" ] || { stat -f %z "$EVENTS" 2>/dev/null > "$OFF" || echo 0 > "$OFF"; }
while :; do
  size=$(stat -f %z "$EVENTS" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  off=$(cat "$OFF" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  [ "$size" -lt "$off" ] && off=0
  if [ "$size" -gt "$off" ]; then
    # consume complete lines only: a trailing partial line (no newline yet) stays
    # unread and the offset stops before it, so it is re-read once its newline lands (robots-97a65)
    tail -c +"$((off + 1))" "$EVENTS" | head -c "$((size - off))" > "$CHUNK"
    len=$(wc -c < "$CHUNK" | tr -d ' ')
    used=$len
    [ -n "$(tail -c 1 "$CHUNK")" ] && used=$((len - $(tail -n 1 "$CHUNK" | wc -c | tr -d ' ')))
    if [ "$used" -gt 0 ]; then
      head -c "$used" "$CHUNK" | while IFS= read -r -u 3 line; do
        id=$(printf '%s' "$line" | sed -n 's/.*"id" *: *"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
        [ -n "$id" ] || continue
        title=$(inbox show "$id" 2>/dev/null | head -1 | cut -c1-160)
        if printf '%s' "$line" | grep -q '"type" *: *"comment"'; then
          n=$(printf '%s' "$line" | sed -n 's/.*"comment_count" *: *\([0-9][0-9]*\).*/\1/p')
          [ -n "$n" ] || continue
          FM_HOME=$FM_HOME "$FM_HOME/bin/fm-inbox.sh" note --request-id "parlay-inbox-$id-c$n" -- \
            "New COMMENT on inbox bead $id (comment $n): ${title:-(title unavailable)}. Re-read the bead (ssh mini1 inbox show $id) and act on the newest comment." >/dev/null 2>&1 \
            || exit 1
          continue
        fi
        FM_HOME=$FM_HOME "$FM_HOME/bin/fm-inbox.sh" note --request-id "parlay-inbox-$id" -- \
          "New Parlay inbox bead $id arrived: ${title:-(title unavailable)}. Triage it per the inbox bead's own description." >/dev/null 2>&1 \
          || exit 1
      done 3<&0 </dev/null  # batch on fd 3; body stdin is /dev/null so ssh-backed calls can't drain it (robots-xcay2)
      # only advance if every note was filed (a failure above exits this subshell, not the loop)
      [ "${PIPESTATUS[1]:-0}" -eq 0 ] && echo "$((off + used))" > "$OFF"
    fi
  fi
  sleep 2
2:# fm-inbox.sh - the captain's out-of-band capture surface.
4:# Solves three DIFFERENT problems with three different mechanisms, because they
5:# are not the same problem:
7:#   note    Queue an idea for firstmate while firstmate is mid-turn and cannot
8:#           answer. Writes a durable record and appends ONE `check` wake, so the
9:#           note survives a crash and is presented at firstmate's next drain.
10:#           `announce` may append that same wake for an already-saved note.
11:#           These two are the only subcommands that touch firstmate's wake queue.
12:#   say     Same as `note`, but the body comes from spoken audio on stdin.
13:#           Speech is an INPUT METHOD here, not an architecture: it transcribes
14:#           and then takes exactly the `note` path.
15:#   status  Answer "what is happening" from durable records ONLY. Reads no
16:#           network and appends NO wake, so it never interrupts work and is safe
17:#           to run in a loop.
18:#   ask     Answer a side question with a one-shot model call that never touches
19:#           firstmate, the backlog, or the wake queue. A side question is not
20:#           fleet work and must not become fleet work.
22:# Usage:
23:#   fm-inbox.sh note [--request-id <id>] [--json] [--] <text>...
24:#   fm-inbox.sh note [--request-id <id>] [--json] -   (body from stdin)
25:#   fm-inbox.sh announce [--json] <id>
26:#   fm-inbox.sh reply [--json] <id> <text>... | reply [--json] <id> -

Captain, here is how the note that tells me to check the inbox gets to me. I read the watcher script and the `fm-inbox.sh` header to confirm each step.

1. **A bead lands.** Your capture or a share creates a bead in the inbox store. The store appends one JSON line to `~/data/inbox/events.jsonl`.
2. **The watcher tails that file.** `fm-parlay-inbox-watch.sh` (in coder-ops) checks every 2 seconds and reads from a saved byte offset. For each new complete line it looks up the bead title. It then files one note through `fm-inbox.sh note --request-id parlay-inbox-<id>`. The request id means a repeat never files a second note. A new comment on an existing bead files its own note.
3. **The note queues a wake.** `fm-inbox.sh note` writes a durable record and appends one `check` wake to my queue. Nothing is lost if I'm mid-turn or crash.
4. **A second path polls.** `inbox-store-watch.check.sh` lists open inbox beads and wakes me on any id it hasn't seen. That is the "new inbox store bead(s) from captain" message.
5. **The stop hook forces the handling turn.** When I try to end a turn with a wake pending, the stop hook blocks it with "captain inbox note pending: inbox:<id>". I then run `fm-wake-drain.sh` and read the note. After handling it I ack with `fm-inbox.sh drain --ack <id>` and the printed `--ack-through` command.

#!/bin/bash
# Build an ad-hoc-signed .ipa and publish it as an OTA (itms-services) install
# package: manifest.plist + index.html + the .ipa, dropped into a served
# folder (default ~/ota). Reach it over Tailscale with `tailscale serve` and
# install by tapping the link in Safari on the iPhone — see AGENTS.md for the
# one-time human setup (MagicDNS/HTTPS Certificates, tailscale serve).
#
# Requires: paid Apple Developer Program team TV2582LRYN already configured
# in TinyKeyboard.xcodeproj (ad-hoc profiles valid ~1yr, not 7 days), `jq`, and
# the `tailscale` CLI logged in on this Mac (only when OTA_BASE_URL is unset —
# it's what the default base URL is derived from).
set -e

PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
SCHEME="TinyKeyboard"
BUNDLE_ID="com.trillium.TinyKeyboard"
TITLE="TinyKeyboard"
OTA_DIR="${OTA_DIR:-$HOME/ota}"

cd "$PROJECT_DIR"

REQUIRED_TOOLS="jq xcodebuild"
# Only the derived-hostname path needs the tailscale CLI; an explicit
# OTA_BASE_URL (alternate port, subpath mount, non-tailnet host) doesn't.
[ -n "${OTA_BASE_URL:-}" ] || REQUIRED_TOOLS="tailscale $REQUIRED_TOOLS"
for tool in $REQUIRED_TOOLS; do
  command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "error: required tool not found on PATH: $tool" >&2; exit 1; }
done

mkdir -p "$OTA_DIR"

# Build artifacts (the .xcarchive, export dir, dSYMs, and the ad-hoc
# embedded.mobileprovision) must never land inside OTA_DIR: that whole
# folder is served over the tailnet, and http.server's directory listing
# doesn't hide dotfiles.
BUILD_DIR="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tinykeyboard-ota-build.XXXXXX")"
trap 'rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR"' EXIT
ARCHIVE_PATH="$BUILD_DIR/TinyKeyboard.xcarchive"
EXPORT_PATH="$BUILD_DIR/export"

# Where the published files will be reachable from the iPhone. Defaults to this
# Mac's tailnet root (derived, never hardcoded). Override OTA_BASE_URL when the
# HTTPS root is already serving something else — e.g. an alternate port
# (https://<mac>.<tailnet>.ts.net:8443) or a subpath mount
# (https://<mac>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ota). See AGENTS.md.
if [ -n "${OTA_BASE_URL:-}" ]; then
  # Strip trailing slashes so composed URLs never contain '//'.
  while [ "${OTA_BASE_URL%/}" != "$OTA_BASE_URL" ]; do OTA_BASE_URL="${OTA_BASE_URL%/}"; done
  case "$OTA_BASE_URL" in
    https://*) ;;
    *)
      echo "error: OTA_BASE_URL must start with 'https://' (got: $OTA_BASE_URL)" >&2
      echo "       iOS refuses itms-services manifests over plain HTTP, so the install would fail silently on the phone." >&2
      exit 1
      ;;
  esac
else
  # Derive this Mac's tailnet hostname instead of hardcoding a machine name.
  HOST="$(tailscale status --json | jq -r '.Self.DNSName | rtrimstr(".")')"
  if [ -z "$HOST" ] || [ "$HOST" = "null" ]; then
    echo "error: could not determine tailnet hostname from 'tailscale status --json' (.Self.DNSName)" >&2
    echo "       is tailscale running and logged in, and is MagicDNS enabled for this tailnet?" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  OTA_BASE_URL="https://$HOST"
fi

# Bump the build number so iOS's OTA installer doesn't silently no-op when
# reinstalling what looks like the same version.
BUNDLE_VERSION="$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)"

# mcpjungle-proxy - answers 405 for the SSE GET leg that coder blocks on.
#
# WHY: coder's MCP client opens GET /mcp (the SSE stream) as part of its
# handshake and blocks on it with a hardcoded 10s deadline. MCPJungle holds the
# stream open, correctly, for minutes - measured 4m6s for coder's own
# connection - so the handshake never completes and coder skips the server with
# "context deadline exceeded".
#
# The MCP spec permits a server to answer that GET with 405 when it does not
# support server-initiated messages. Caddy enforces exactly that here, then
# passes every other request through unchanged, including streaming POST
# responses.
#
# NOT a workaround for a bug in either project: it resolves one optional
# protocol leg the two disagree about, in the only place both can be left alone.
#
# UPSTREAM: 127.0.0.1:8337 is com.mcpjungle.session-proxy, which logs the
# Mcp-Session-Id, client address and MCP error for every request before
# forwarding it to MCPJungle on 127.0.0.1:8338. It exists because MCPJungle v0.4.6
# has no per-request session log, so a client reporting "session terminated"
# could not be diagnosed. Its log is
# ~/.local/share/mcpjungle/session-proxy.jsonl. To bypass the logger and restore
# the direct hop, point upstream back at 127.0.0.1:8338 and reload Caddy.

:8339 {
	@mcp_sse {
		method GET
		path /mcp
	}
	respond @mcp_sse 405

	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8337 {
		# stream responses through rather than buffering them
		flush_interval -1
	}
}

- **Firstmate Share:** the address will be built in, and the secret will be loaded into the app's own secure storage the first time it opens. You open the app and it works, with no Settings step.
- **Safety:** the secret goes into the build from a local file on the MacBook and is never committed to git. The repo's secret scanner must still pass.
- **Talon palette:** I told the worker to prefill anything the palette asks for too, but I don't know yet whether it has settings.

why csnt that stuff be passed as build args?

Captain, it can be passed as build arguments, and that's roughly what I asked for. The worker will probably use exactly that.

With xcodebuild, you pass settings on the command line, for example `FMS_ENDPOINT=https://macbook.hippo-tilapia.ts.net:8771/share FMS_SECRET=$(cat ~/.config/firstmate-share/secret)`. Those become Info.plist values, so the app reads them at launch and stores the secret in the Keychain.

- **Why not just commit them?** The secret in git is what's forbidden. A build argument never touches git, because it's read from the local secret file at build time.
- **The one tradeoff:** the secret ends up inside the installed app bundle on your phone. For a personal app on your own device, that's fine.
- **The endpoint:** this one isn't sensitive, so it can be a default committed in the repo.

I'll steer the worker to use build arguments rather than a generated file if it picked the file route. It's the simpler approach, and `make install` would just pass them in. I'll confirm what it did when it reports back.

# Receiver (MacBook side)

The phone POSTs a share to the MacBook; the receiver files an inbox-store bead; `inbox-wake-poll` puts it on
`~/data/inbox/events.jsonl`; `fm-parlay-inbox-watch.sh` wakes firstmate with a note. Code: `receiver/fms_receiver.py`.

## Trust model (steer-560)
The tailnet is trusted. `tailscale serve` adds `Tailscale-User-Login` / `Tailscale-User-Name` to every request it
proxies from a tailnet user's node, and strips copies the client sent. A `POST /share` that carries that login is
accepted with no secret. A request without it (direct loopback, a tagged node) still needs
`Authorization: Bearer <secret>`, so curl-from-localhost with the secret keeps working.
The receiver never binds beyond loopback and is never on Funnel, so only serve can reach it from off the Mac. A process
on this Mac could forge the header on loopback, but it runs as the same user and could read the secret file anyway.

## Layout
| Piece | Where |
|---|---|
| Process | launchd `com.firstmateshare.receiver`, `/usr/bin/python3`, bound to `127.0.0.1:8770` only |
| Public face | `tailscale serve --http=8774` and `--https=8771` -> loopback. Tailnet only; install refuses if Funnel is on, and never replaces a serve port another service holds |

- **What can't move:** Talon's own speech recognizer runs only on the Mac, so it can't be ported to the iPhone.

result.output:
1	# Scout: can Talon's speech layer move to the iPhone?
2	
3	**Short answer:** Not as a port. Talon's recognizer is a Mac-only Conformer (wav2letter-format) engine with a native decoder dylib, and there is no iOS build of it in the install. What *can* move to the phone is the transcription step itself: an on-device Whisper-class or Apple SpeechAnalyzer model on the iPhone produces text, and Talon consumes that text as a phrase. Talon already has a text-in path (`speech_system.engine_mimic`, `actions.mimic`) and an engine-plugin seam (`add_engine`), so the integration surface exists. The recommended next step is a small latency/WER experiment on a real iPhone, described in section 6.
4	
5	Scope: report only. No code, grammar, or Talon voice commands were changed. The only scratch activity was read-only inspection of `~/.talon`, the Talon app bundle, and this worktree, plus web searches. Nothing was pushed and no PR was opened.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. What Talon's speech engine is
10	
11	**Engine family.** The repo README says Talon's recommended engine is its "built-in Conformer (wav2letter) speech recognition engine" (`README.md:21`). The running engine is the w2l engine: the Talon watchdog log repeatedly reports stacks through `talon/engines/w2l.py:730` and `talon/scripting/dispatch.py:132` (`~/.talon/talon.log`, watchdog lines dated 2026-10-18). Dragon is the other option (`README.md:21`, `~/.talon/documentation/engines/dragon/DraconityClient.md`), but it is Windows/discontinued on Mac and is not the active engine here.
12	
13	**Models on disk.** Talon's blob store is `~/.talon/.sys/blob/`, and its keyval DB (`~/.talon/.sys/user.db`, table `keyval`) records which models are registered:
14	
15	- `sys.w2l.models` lists three model ids: `19a05637…`, `2285dbfb…`, `f7e58e5a…`.
16	- `sys.speech.engine-mru` orders the engines as `wav2letter` (most recent, 2026-03-08) then `wav2letter-conformer` (2026-03-07).
17	
18	The manifests, read directly from the blob store:
19	
20	| Manifest (`blob/…`) | Name | Blobs |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| `19/19a05637…` | **Conformer D (2025-01-06)**, en_US, most recently used | `acoustic.onnx` 111.4 MB (ONNX, PyTorch-exported; header is `pytorch`), `lexicon.txt` 4.35 MB, `lexicon_flat.bin` 12.1 MB |
23	| `f7/f7e58e5a…` | Conformer D (2023-05-20) + Whisper, not public | `acoustic.b2l` 111 MB (`BW2L` format), `ort.patch` 164 KB, lexicon files, `whisper-tiny.bin` 78 MB, `whisper-base.bin` 148 MB, `whisper-small.bin` 488 MB (ggml, `lmgg` magic), `measure.flac` 129 KB |
24	| `6d/6d4da3d8…` | Conformer D (2023-05-20) | `acoustic.b2l`, `ort.patch`, lexicon files |
25	
26	Which manifest is live is inferred from the MRU timestamps, not confirmed by a live query. Verify with `settings.get` or the REPL if it matters.
27	
28	**Key takeaways about the engine:**
29	
30	- The acoustic model is an ONNX graph run through ONNX Runtime (`~/.talon/documentation/engines/w2l/W2lOrtEncoder.md:5`, `W2lModelInfo` fields `model_format`, `am_path`, `ort_patch`, `whisper_paths`, `measure_path`: `W2lModelInfo.md:5`).
31	- Decoding uses a native library, `/Applications/Talon.app/Contents/Frameworks/libw2ldecode.dylib`, which contains `w2l::` symbols (TrieNode, FlatTrie, LM, ZeroLM). It exists only in the Mac app bundle, and `Talon 2.app` has its own copy. Nothing in the bundle or on disk is an iOS build.
32	- The Whisper `.bin` files are bundled in Talon's own manifest. The w2l model config has a `whisper_paths` field, which suggests Whisper is used inside the Talon engine (perhaps for rescoring). I did **not** verify how Talon uses them at runtime.
33	- `sys.speech.record_all` is `true` (`user.db`). Talon is saving every utterance: `~/.talon/recordings/` holds 329,247 FLAC files (8.0 GB), with the phrase in each filename. This is a large local audio corpus. It is the captain's voice and must stay local; do not publish or ship it.
34	
35	Note: `~/.talon/documentation` is auto-generated API stubs. Most method pages have `None` for their description, so the source of truth is the bundled API docs plus the repo's own usage.
36	
37	## 2. What Talon exposes for external recognition input
38	
39	The `speech_system` API (`~/.talon/documentation_clean/talon_complete_api_docs_clean.md`, section `speech_system`, from line 9222):
40	
41	| API | Line | What it does |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| `add_engine(engine: AbstractEngine)` | 9228 | Attaches a recognizer. An engine is any `AbstractEngine` subclass. |
44	| `remove_engine(engine)` | 9282 | Detaches one. |
45	| `pick_engine()` | 9276 | Chooses the active engine. |
46	| `engine_mimic(phrase)` | 9252 | Sends a phrase as if an engine recognized it. |
47	| `parse(phrase)` | 9266 | Parses a phrase against the grammar and returns the capture and match. |
48	| `engine_event(topic, engine, j)` | 9239 | Engines post events (e.g. recognized phrases) into the pipeline. |
49	| `_sim(phrase)` | used at `trillium/palette_feed/palette_feed.py:114` | Simulates a phrase and returns the match text. Raises `RuntimeError("Failed to parse")` on no match (per `CLAUDE.md`, "Talon runtime facts"). |
50	
51	Existing repo code already uses these:
52	
53	- `core/dragon_engine.py:10-22` calls `speech_system.engine_mimic("go to sleep")` and similar, so this path is in active use.
54	- `trillium/palette_feed/palette_feed.py:120-128`: `execute()` runs `actions.mimic(phrase)` on Talon's main thread. The file's comment at line 121 says that with no engine attached, `actions.mimic` "neither raises nor dispatches", so `engine_active()` checks `scope.get("speech.engine")` first. An external recognizer therefore has to be attached (`add_engine`) before text input does anything.
55	- `palette_feed` already accepts a phrase over HTTP on port 7399 and feeds it to `actions.mimic`. Auth is gated by `TALON_PALETTE_OPEN_EXECUTE` (`docs/palette-feed.md`, lines 6-15). This is the existing phone-to-Talon transport, so a phone-side transcript could reuse it instead of building a new one.
56	
57	Precedent for replacing the engine entirely: the Dragon engine runs outside Talon and talks over a socket. `DraconityClient(connector: Callable[[], SocketType], secret: str)` (`~/.talon/documentation/engines/dragon/DraconityClient.md:5`). That is the template for an out-of-process recognizer.
58	
59	What text input loses versus the Conformer. `trillium/core/on_phrase/analyze_phrase/analyze_phrase.py` reads per-word `start`/`end` timing and `WordMeta` (`analyze_phrase.py:15`, `get_words` and `get_metadata`). Phrases from `engine_mimic` or `actions.mimic` have no audio timing and no decode confidence, so those features return `None`. Grammar matching works on the phrase text, so commands should still match. I did not test this on a live Talon; it follows from the API shape.
60	
61	## 3. Can Talon's model run on iOS?
62	
63	Not directly. Evidence:
64	
65	- The engine depends on `libw2ldecode.dylib` (Mac only, see section 1) and on Talon's own Python runtime (`talon.engines.w2l`, which is not in any iOS-capable package).
66	- The acoustic model is ONNX (`acoustic.onnx`). In principle ONNX can run on iOS (ONNX Runtime and sherpa-onnx both target iOS), but the Conformer weights and Talon's decode graph (lexicon trie, KenLM-style LM in `lmgg` blobs) would have to be ported. That is a multi-week effort with no published guarantee.
67	- The Talon engine would also need its custom decoder rewritten. I found no evidence that Talon's Conformer has been exported to Core ML.
68	
69	Verdict: porting the Talon Conformer is not a reasonable path. Use a different on-device recognizer and feed its text to Talon.
70	
71	## 4. On-device options for iPhone
72	
73	**A. Apple SpeechAnalyzer (iOS 26+).** Runs fully on device; the model is managed by the OS.
74	
75	- Modules: `SpeechTranscriber` (long-form), `DictationTranscriber` (short utterances), `SpeechDetector` (VAD). Source: [Apple SpeechAnalyzer overview, via addpipe blog](https://blog.addpipe.com/apple-speechanalyzer-api/), [blakecrosley comparison](https://blakecrosley.com/blog/speech-framework-vs-sfspeechrecognizer).
76	- Accuracy: a third-party LibriSpeech run on an M2 Pro reported WER 2.12% clean and 4.56% noisy. This is not an Apple number. Source: [developersdigest benchmark](https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/apple-speechanalyzer-vs-whisper-benchmark), [gigazine](https://www.gigazine.net/gsc_news/en/20250619-apple-speech-analyzer).
77	- Gap: no custom vocabulary. This matters for Talon's command vocabulary, but command matching happens in Talon's grammar on the Mac, so the phone only needs open-vocabulary transcription.
78	- Unverified: whether `requiresOnDeviceRecognition` exists on `SpeechAnalyzer`. It exists on the legacy `SFSpeechRecognitionRequest` (only effective when `supportsOnDeviceRecognition` is true), per search results I could not confirm against Apple's docs. Check the iOS 26 SDK header before relying on it.
79	
80	**B. WhisperKit (Argmax, Core ML).** Swift package, MIT license, runs Whisper on the Neural Engine via Core ML, with streaming, word timestamps, and VAD. Source: [Argmax open-source SDK](https://docsearch.algolia.com/mcp/docs/repo/argmaxinc/argmax-oss-swift), [WhisperKit listing](https://www.sourcepulse.org/projects/1255576). Canonical repo: `github.com/argmaxinc/WhisperKit`. Models come from `argmaxinc/whisperkit-coreml` on Hugging Face. The search results did not state a minimum iOS version; check the README.
81	
82	**C. whisper.cpp (ggml, with optional Core ML encoder).** Same Whisper weights as Talon's bundled `whisper-*.bin`, so it reuses what Talon already ships. Source: [ggml-org/whisper.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp).
83	
84	- The README claims the Core ML encoder is more than 3x faster than CPU (project claim, no benchmark found).
85	- Latency data point (via the whisper.rn wrapper, not native): tiny.en with Core ML handles a 30-second clip in about 800 ms on an iPhone 13 Pro Max. Source: [whisper.rn optimization docs](https://www.mintlify.com/mybigday/whisper.rn/advanced/optimization).
86	- First launch is much slower, because the ANE compiles the model to a device-specific format.
87	
88	**D. sherpa-onnx (k2-fsa).** Pre-built iOS binaries; React Native wrapper lists iOS as production-ready (min iOS 13) with Core ML, NNAPI, XNNPACK, and QNN execution providers. Streaming models are Zipformer, Paraformer, and CTC. I found no streaming Conformer in the listing. Smallest English streaming Zipformer is about 20M parameters. Sources: [react-native-sherpa-onnx](https://www.mintlify.com/xdcobra/react-native-sherpa-onnx), [sherpa-onnx README](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx@master/README.md). No iPhone benchmark found.
89	
90	**Already on this Mac:** SuperWhisper runs Whisper-small (`ggml-small.bin`, plus `vad-v2.onnx` and `emb-v1.onnx`) from `~/Library/Application Support/superwhisper/`. Talon log lines show it being used ("submit SuperWhisper", 2026-10-18). This is evidence that Whisper-small is already working on this machine, so it is a usable accuracy baseline.
91	
92	## 5. Latency and accuracy tradeoffs
93	
94	| Option | Runs on iPhone | Latency evidence | Accuracy evidence | Notes |
95	|---|---|---|---|---|
96	| Talon Conformer (current, Mac) | No | Not measured here | Not measured here | Has timing and confidence that text input loses |
97	| SpeechAnalyzer (iOS 26) | Yes | Not found | Third-party LibriSpeech WER 2.12% (M2 Pro) | No custom vocabulary |
98	| WhisperKit small/base | Yes | Not found for iPhone | Whisper-class; no iPhone WER found | Needs Core ML download; ANE warm-up |
99	| whisper.cpp tiny.en + Core ML | Yes | ~800 ms per 30 s clip, iPhone 13 Pro Max (aggregator) | Whisper tiny, weaker than small | Reuses Talon's bundled `whisper-tiny.bin` |
100	| sherpa-onnx streaming Zipformer small | Yes | Not found | Not found | True streaming, partials; no Conformer |
101	
102	Accuracy numbers in this table are not comparable across rows (different datasets, no shared test set). That is why the experiment in section 6 matters.
103	
104	Tradeoff in short: streaming (sherpa-onnx, SpeechAnalyzer) gives partial results and lower perceived latency. Whisper-class batch models are more accurate on general speech but need an endpoint (VAD) to know when an utterance ended. For short voice commands, the endpoint is the dominant latency term, not the decode.
105	
106	## 6. Recommended minimal experiment
107	
108	Goal: decide whether phone transcription plus Talon text injection beats the Mac Conformer on command accuracy and end-to-end latency. Do not change Talon's grammar or commands.
109	
110	1. Build a labelled test set of about 200 command utterances. Use a hand-labelled subset from `~/.talon/recordings/`. The filenames are Talon's own recognition output, not ground truth, so correct each label by hand. Keep the audio local.
111	2. Run the same clips through three transcribers on the iPhone or on the Mac: WhisperKit `small` (or whisper.cpp `small` with Core ML), SpeechAnalyzer `DictationTranscriber`, and sherpa-onnx streaming Zipformer small. Measure WER on the command phrases and time from end-of-speech to text.
112	3. Run the same clips through Talon's Conformer for a baseline. Record its output with the existing `speech_system._sim` path (or the REPL) against the hand labels.
113	4. Measure the injection leg separately: phone text → HTTP → `actions.mimic`. Use `palette_feed` as the transport. Time it on the LAN and over the tailnet.
114	5. Decision rule: if the best phone option is within a few points of the Conformer on command WER and end-to-end latency is under about 1 s, a prototype `AbstractEngine` (added with `add_engine`, out-of-process like Dragon) is worth building. Otherwise keep the Mac engine.
115	
116	Test cost is small: one Swift test app for WhisperKit and SpeechAnalyzer, plus a clip replay script on the Mac.
117	
118	## 7. Recommendation
119	
120	1. Do not port Talon's Conformer to iOS. Its decoder is a Mac dylib and the port is large.
121	2. If the goal is phone-side speech, pair an on-device Whisper-class or SpeechAnalyzer transcriber on the iPhone with Talon's existing text entry (`engine_mimic` / `actions.mimic`, transport already in `palette_feed`).
122	3. Run the section 6 experiment before committing to an `AbstractEngine` implementation.
123	
124	**Note:** The `recordings/` corpus is the captain's voice. Keep it on the Mac and out of any phone or cloud pipeline unless he agrees.
125	
126	## Evidence index
127	
128	- `README.md:21`: Conformer as recommended engine.
129	- `~/.talon/talon.log`: watchdog stacks at `talon/engines/w2l.py:730`, `talon/scripting/dispatch.py:132`.
130	- `~/.talon/.sys/user.db` keyval: `sys.w2l.models`, `sys.speech.engine-mru`, `sys.speech.engine_id-mru`, `sys.speech.record_all`.
131	- `~/.talon/.sys/blob/19/19a05637…`, `blob/f7/f7e58e5a…`, `blob/6d/6d4da3d8…`: model manifests.
132	- `~/.talon/.sys/blob/50/50648466…` (`pytorch` header), `blob/14/1487762f…` and `blob/b2/b215cd26…` (`BW2L` header), `blob/60/60ed5bc3…`, `blob/be/be07e048…`, `blob/1b/1be3a9b2…` (`lmgg` headers).
133	- `~/.talon/documentation/engines/w2l/W2lModelInfo.md:5`, `W2lOrtEncoder.md:5`.
134	- `~/.talon/documentation/engines/dragon/DraconityClient.md:5`.
135	- `~/.talon/documentation_clean/talon_complete_api_docs_clean.md:9222-9300` (speech_system API), `:6354` (W2lEngine).
136	- `/Applications/Talon.app/Contents/Frameworks/libw2ldecode.dylib`: decoder, Mac-only.
137	- `core/dragon_engine.py:10-22`: `engine_mimic` usage.
138	- `trillium/palette_feed/palette_feed.py:112-128`: `sim`, `engine_active`, `execute` via `actions.mimic`.
139	- `trillium/core/on_phrase/analyze_phrase/analyze_phrase.py:15`: word timing and `WordMeta` consumers.

141	- `~/Library/Application Support/superwhisper/`: Whisper-small already in use on the Mac.
142

Captain, you may be right to push back. The scout's "can't port" is an inference from reading files. It never tried a port or ran anything.

**What it found:**
1. **The model:** Talon's current speech model is "Conformer D (2025-01-06)". Its core is a 111 MB `acoustic.onnx` file, which is a standard ONNX model. Talon also ships three bundled Whisper models (tiny, base and small), but the scout didn't verify how Talon uses them.
2. **The parts that tie it to the Mac:**
   - **Decoder:** it is `libw2ldecode.dylib`, a Mac-only library in the Talon app.
   - **Runtime:** it runs inside Talon's own Python runtime.
   - **Language model:** the word-prediction data is a custom format.
   
   The scout found no iPhone build and no sign anyone has exported it for iPhone.
3. **Why it called a port unreasonable:** the ONNX model could in principle run on iOS. Porting the decoder and the word-prediction data would be "multi-week, no guarantee". That estimate is unmeasured, so it's a weak spot.
4. **How text gets into Talon:** Talon already accepts text as if spoken (`engine_mimic` and `actions.mimic`), and it has a plug-in point for a different recognizer (`add_engine`). The Dragon engine is an existing example of a recognizer that runs outside Talon and talks to it over a socket.
5. **What text input loses:** per-word timing and confidence, because the scout read that some of your code uses them. This was not tested on a live Talon.
6. **Phone options:**

   | Option | Notes |
   |---|---|
   | Apple's on-device speech feature (iOS 26) | No custom vocabulary. A third-party test measured a 2.1% word error rate on clean speech, on a Mac. |
   | WhisperKit | Runs Whisper on the iPhone's Neural Engine. |
   | whisper.cpp | A 30-second clip took about 800 ms on an iPhone 13 Pro Max, via a wrapper library. |
   | sherpa-onnx | Streaming, iPhone-ready. |

   No iPhone accuracy or speed numbers were found for most of these.
7. **Experiment it proposed:** take about 200 of your hand-labelled commands from `~/.talon/recordings/` (329,247 clips, 8 GB, your voice, kept local). Run them through the phone options and through Talon, and time the phone-to-Talon send. If a phone option is within a few points on accuracy and under about 1 second, build a custom recognizer.

Which part do you disagree with? If it is "can't move", the cheapest test is running Talon's ONNX model on the phone. That would settle whether the decoder is really a blocker. Tell me and I'll dispatch it.

# Scout: Talon's ort.patch, and the split-encoder path for iPhone

Task: inbox-nxny (ort.patch), inbox-7i6u (split encoder). Prior findings: brain-key50, `data/scout-talon-phone-asr/report.md`.
Scope: read-only. Nothing installed, nothing in `~/.talon` changed, nothing run on the iPhone. Scratch files live in the scratchpad, not in the repo or `~/.talon`.

## Verdict

1. **ort.patch is not an ONNX Runtime patch.** It is a bsdiff file that turns the BW2L container `acoustic.b2l` (Conformer D 2023) into an ONNX model. It is not load-bearing for the live `acoustic.onnx`, and it does not make the model run on iOS.
2. **The real load blocker is not in the patch.** The ONNX graph calls a `com.microsoft:PowerSpectrum` custom op. Stock ONNX Runtime 1.24.1 (the wheel bundled with Talon) refuses to load both `acoustic.onnx` and the ort.patch output. I found no implementation of that op anywhere in the install.
3. **brain-key50 verdict holds: a full port to iOS is not reasonable.** The reason changes. The blockers are (a) the PowerSpectrum kernel, and (b) the decoder, which is a Mac-only dylib with no source here.
4. **Split encoder: viable for the decoder side, not free.** Shipping the 29-dim output logits costs about 12% of raw 16 kHz PCM. Shipping the 256-dim hidden state costs more than raw PCM. The phone still needs the PowerSpectrum kernel, so the split path moves the hard problem to the phone rather than removing it.
5. **Open, and it matters most:** I could not find what runs PowerSpectrum on this Mac. Until that is answered, the claim "Talon's engine loads acoustic.onnx" is unverified.

## What I did

- Read the manifests and blobs in `~/.talon/.sys/blob/` and checked their SHA-256 values.
- Parsed the bsdiff control stream (`scratchpad/bsdiff_inspect.py`), applied the patch (`scratchpad/bspatch_apply.py`), and compared the output with `acoustic.onnx` byte for byte.
- Parsed the ONNX protobuf directly, without ORT (`scratchpad/onnx_graph_io.py`, `onnx_chain.py`, `onnx_scan.py`), using Talon's bundled Python 3.14 (`/Applications/Talon.app/Contents/Resources/python/bin/python3 -I`).
- Tried to load both models with Talon's bundled ORT 1.24.1 (`scratchpad/ort_probe.py`). This loads but does not run inference.
- Searched the Talon app bundle, `~/.talon`, and `talon.log` for PowerSpectrum, ORT symbols, and model-load lines.
- Read the W2L docs in `~/.talon/documentation/engines/w2l/` and listed `libw2ldecode.dylib` exports with `/usr/bin/nm`.

Not done: running inference (blocked by PowerSpectrum), any iOS build, and any latency measurement.

Two of my `nm -gU …` calls therefore sent their arguments to Talon's speech input. Talon logged "failed to parse phrase" for `['-gU', '']`, so no command appears to have fired, but this was not verified for the second c

## 1. What ort.patch is

Evidence:

- Manifest `~/.talon/.sys/blob/6d/6d4da3d8…` (Conformer D 2023-05-20) lists `ort.patch` as `40/4010086318089b8b…`, 164,011 bytes, and `acoustic.b2l` as `14/1487762f…`, 110,972,818 bytes.
- The patch header is `BSDIFF40`, with control, diff and extra blocks bz2-compressed.
- Control stream: 6,032 entries. `newsize` = 111,421,755. The largest old-file offset read = 110,972,818, which is exactly the size of `acoustic.b2l`. So the old file is the b2l.
- The diff block is 111,029,529 bytes, and every byte is zero. The extra block is 392,226 bytes. So the output is the b2l's bytes with 392 KB of literal insertions and replacements.
- Applying the patch gives a file with `pytorch` ONNX header, 111,421,755 bytes. `cmp` against `acoustic.onnx` (sha `50648466…`, 111,421,844 bytes) shows zero differences over the 111,421,755 bytes. The 2025 file has 89 extra bytes at the end: `metadata_props` with `tokens` (`|`, `'`, `a`–`z`, `#`) and `type=conformer`.
- Talon's binary contains the string `BSDIFF40` (`MacOS/Talon`), so Talon applies this itself at runtime.

Conclusion: ort.patch rebuilds the ONNX graph for the 2023 manifest from the b2l container. It patches Talon's model bytes, not ORT. The name is misleading.

## 2. Is it load-bearing for acoustic.onnx?

- **Live model:** the 2025 manifest `19/19a05637…` points to `acoustic.onnx` (sha `50648466…`) directly. It has no ort.patch entry. So for that manifest the patch is not needed.
- **2023 manifest:** the patch is needed only if Talon uses the BW2L path. Which manifest is live is inferred from MRU timestamps in `user.db`, not confirmed by a live query. Verify with `settings.get` or the REPL.
- **Does it change what ORT can load?** No. Both files fail in the same way (below).

## 3. Can ORT load acoustic.onnx? (PowerSpectrum)

Command: `python -I ort_probe.py acoustic_2025.onnx patched_out.bin` with Talon's bundled `onnxruntime 1.24.1`.

Result, same for both files:

```
[ONNXRuntimeError] : 1 : FAIL : … failed:Node (If_16) Op (If) [TypeInferenceError]
Graph attribute inferencing failed: Fatal error: com.microsoft:PowerSpectrum(-1) is not a registered function/op
```

Graph facts (from the protobuf walk, `onnx_graph_io.py`):

- ir_version 7. Opset imports: `ai.onnx` 13, `com.microsoft` 1.
- 4,960 standard nodes and 1 `com.microsoft:PowerSpectrum` node, inside an `If` subgraph (`If:525`, node 697) with `nfft = 512`.
- Input: `input`, element type float32 (1), shape `[in_sequence]`. **The model takes a raw waveform of variable length.** The spectrogram front-end is inside the graph.
- Output: `output`, float32, declared rank 4 `[batch_size, Addoutput_dim_1, Addoutput_dim_2, out_sequence]`. Its producer is `Add` (node 4677), fed by `MatMul` with weight `[256, 29]` and bias `[29]`. So the last axis is **29**, which matches the 29 tokens in `tokens`.
- 874 initializers, 17 `Conv` nodes.

Searches for an implementation of PowerSpectrum:

| Where | Result |
|---|---|
| `MacOS/Talon` | 0 matches |
| `Frameworks/libw2ldecode.dylib`, `libdraconity.dylib` | 0 matches |
| `site-packages/onnxruntime/capi/onnxruntime_pybind11_state.so` | 0 matches (ORT has `com.microsoft` strings, 11 hits) |
| `site-packages/onnxruntime_extensions` | 0 matches |
| `~/.talon` (excluding recordings and blob) | 0 matches |
| `talon.log` | No model-load lines at all, only palette-feed lines |

So the live w2l engine (watchdog stacks at `talon/engines/w2l.py:730`) must load this model in some way I could not find. Possibilities: a kernel compiled into the Talon binary under a name I did not search, a separate ORT build, or the engine does not load this file. **This is the top open item.**

**iOS implication:** ORT iOS can load the model only after a PowerSpectrum kernel is registered (a custom op library built for iOS, or a replacement that computes a 512-point power spectrum). That kernel is small. The bigger question is whether the front-end should stay in the graph.

# Scout: what implements com.microsoft:PowerSpectrum for Talon's acoustic.onnx

Related beads: inbox-1i4c, brain-gjqec, brain-key50. Prior scout: `data/talon-ort-split-scout/report.md`.
Scope: read-only. Nothing installed, nothing in `~/.talon` changed, no mimic, nothing run on the iPhone. Scratch scripts live in the worktree scratchpad, not in the repo or `~/.talon`.

## Verdict

1. **No implementation of PowerSpectrum exists anywhere I could read.** It is absent from `Talon.app` (native binaries, dylibs, bundled Python site-packages), from `~/.talon` (excluding recordings and the blob store), from the ORT pybind `.so`, and from the onnxruntime-extensions `.so`. Public search also found no definition of it.
2. **The gap is in the engine code, and that code is encrypted.** Talon's engine modules (`talon/engines/w2l.py4`, `talon/nn/w2l/b2l.py4`, `talon/nn/w2l/feature.py4`, `talon/plugins/engines/w2l.py4`) are not plaintext Python. The first bytes are high-entropy binary. A grep cannot see inside them, so a Python-side op registration would be invisible to every search above. I did not try to decrypt them.
3. **The live Talon process loads the bundled ORT 1.24.1 Python wheel, not a custom ORT build.** The Talon binary links no ORT. The running process maps only `onnxruntime_pybind11_state.so` and `_extensions_pydll…so`, and neither contains `PowerSpectrum`. So if the engine loads `acoustic.onnx`, it registers the op from Python, which I cannot verify. **Still open.**
4. **The op is almost certainly a one-sided power spectrum of a Hamming-windowed frame, which standard ONNX ops can reproduce.** The graph pins the window (400 samples), the FFT size (512), and the output width (257 bins). The exact power-vs-magnitude choice and the hop are still unverified.
5. **New finding: the front end normalises over the whole input, not per frame.** `ReduceMean_195` has no `axes`, so it reduces every axis. A chunked or split encoder would not match offline output unless the statistics are fixed. This matters for the split-encoder design.
6. **Recommendation: do not start an iOS port on this evidence.** The PowerSpectrum rewrite is small, but its exact semantics need checking against Talon's real features first.

## What I did

- Searched `/Applications/Talon.app` for `powerspectrum|power_spectrum` (case-insensitive, binary and text). No matches.
- Searched `~/.talon` for the same, excluding `recordings`, `blob`, and `.git`. No matches.
- Checked `otool -L` on `MacOS/Talon`. No ORT, no custom-op library linked.
- Checked the ORT pybind `.so` and the extensions `.so` for `powerspectrum`. 0 hits each. Extensions contains `LogMelSpectrum` (2 hits), not `PowerSpectrum`.
- Found the live Talon process (pid 16538) and listed its mapped images with `lsof -p 16538`.
- Searched `talon.log` for `w2l`, `onnx`, `acoustic`, `engine`, `model`, `watchdog`. 0 matches.
- Parsed the `acoustic.onnx` protobuf (blob `50/50648466…`) with Talon's bundled Python 3.14 in isolated mode (`python3 -I`). Scripts: `ps_node.py`, `ps_chain.py`, `ps_tensors.py`, `ps_prod.py`, `ps_down.py`, `ps_attr.py`.
- Re-ran the prior ORT load probe (`ort_probe.py`). Load only, no inference.
- Ran two web searches for `PowerSpectrum` and for Talon/w2l references. No relevant hits.

Not done: a live Talon REPL load test (see Recommendations), any inference, any numeric comparison, any iOS work.

Captain, the PowerSpectrum scout is done and its bead (inbox-1i4c) is closed. The `nm` fix is ready and needs your OK to land. The scout found that:
- **No implementation found.** The operation isn't in Talon's app, the `~/.talon` folder, or the runtime's extensions.
- **Talon's speech-engine code is encrypted.** That's the likely place it's registered, so no search can see it.
- **The operation is probably easy to rebuild.** It is almost certainly a standard 512-point power spectrum, which ordinary operations can reproduce. The exact details are unverified.
- **A split-model design has a new problem.** The model normalizes over the whole input, not per chunk. A chunked phone-to-Mac split won't match Talon's output unless that is handled.
- **Recommendation:** don't start an iPhone port yet. First test how Talon loads the model live, tracked as task-u7mzk.

**`nm` fix:** it is committed on the dotfiles branch `fm/dotfiles-nm-q1` (commit 950d67d). It removes the shell function that was hijacking `nm`. A config-only build passed, but nothing is switched on yet. Your shell only picks it up after a rebuild. Dotfiles is local-only, so I haven't landed it. Say the word and I'll land it.

   - No implementation was found. Talon's engine code is encrypted.
   - The operation is probably a standard 512-point power spectrum that ordinary operations can rebuild.
   - The model normalizes over the whole input, which complicates a chunked split.
   - Recommendation: test how Talon loads the model live before any port (task-u7mzk).

Both sets of findings are also posted on brain-key50, the bead for your Dispatch coordination. Their workers are cleaned up. The decisive experiment, getting the acoustic model running on the iPhone, only goes ahead on your word.

# robots-4ayi4 — `bd comment` fails with "embeddeddolt: store is read-only"

Status: diagnosis complete. Read-only; no tracked files changed in the brain worktree.

## Verdict

- **Not caused by the hook-ancestry check.** `insideHook()` / `AncestorRunningHook` produce a different error ("refused: this process was started by a hook"). The "store is read-only" error comes from a read-only store that `comment` opens through **auto-routing**, after the local lookup misses.
- **Store-open mode is not the trigger for local IDs.** `comment` is not in `readOnlyCommands`, and a local ID opens a writable store. The read-only store only appears on the routed path.
- **Real-use impact: yes.** Any user with `beads.role=contributor` (or the URL fallback resolving to contributor) who runs `bd comment <id>` for an ID that lives in the auto-routed planning store gets this error. It is not sandbox-only.
- **Proposed fix:** make the error say what happened (ID lives in a read-only auto-routed store). Do not make auto-routed stores writable: the code says that is intentional (GH#2345, `routed.go:87-88`).

## Root cause chain (with evidence)

1. `comment` resolves its ID with `resolveAndGetIssueForMutation(ctx, store, id)`, `cmd/bd/comment.go:74`.
2. That calls `resolveAndGetIssueWithRoutingAccess(..., writablePrefixRoute=true)`, `cmd/bd/routed.go:66-67`.
   - Local lookup first: `routed.go:72`.
   - On not-found, prefix routing (writable): `routed.go:81`.
   - On not-found, **auto-routing**: `routed.go:89-93`, which calls `resolveViaAutoRouting`, `routed.go:123`.
3. `resolveViaAutoRouting` → `openRoutedReadStore` (`cmd/bd/routing_read.go:96`) → `newReadOnlyStoreFromConfig` (`routing_read.go:104`) → `embeddeddolt.OpenReadOnly` (`cmd/bd/store_factory.go:192`) → store with `readOnly: true` (`internal/storage/embeddeddolt/store.go:129-150`).
4. The issue is found in that store, so `comment` gets it as `result.Store` (`comment.go:89`) and calls `AddIssueComment` (`comment.go:95`).
5. The write goes through `withConn(commit=true)`, which returns `errReadOnly` when `s.readOnly` (`store.go:180-181`). `errReadOnly` text is `embeddeddolt: store is read-only` (`store.go:65`). Message surfaces as `adding comment: ...` (`comment.go:97`).

The routed path is also reached for `comments add` (same `comment.go` / `comments.go:135`).

`determineAutoRoutedRepoPath` (`routing_read.go:50-`) calls `routing.DetectUserRole(".")` (`internal/routing/routing.go:37-62`), which runs `git config --get beads.role` (`routing.go:69-70`).

- Role found (`contributor`): auto-routing picks the planning repo → read-only store → **"store is read-only"**.
- Role not found: bd prints `warning: beads.role not configured (GH#2950)` and falls back to the URL heuristic (`routing.go:60-62`). The ID does not route, so the local miss ends in **"resolving <id>: no issue found matching"** (`comment.go:76`).

fm-inbox.sh - the captain's out-of-band capture surface.

Solves three DIFFERENT problems with three different mechanisms, because they
are not the same problem:

  note    Queue an idea for firstmate while firstmate is mid-turn and cannot
          answer. Writes a durable record and appends ONE `check` wake, so the
          note survives a crash and is presented at firstmate's next drain.
          `announce` may append that same wake for an already-saved note.
          These two are the only subcommands that touch firstmate's wake queue.
  say     Same as `note`, but the body comes from spoken audio on stdin.
          Speech is an INPUT METHOD here, not an architecture: it transcribes
          and then takes exactly the `note` path.
  status  Answer "what is happening" from durable records ONLY. Reads no
          network and appends NO wake, so it never interrupts work and is safe
          to run in a loop.
  ask     Answer a side question with a one-shot model call that never touches
          firstmate, the backlog, or the wake queue. A side question is not
          fleet work and must not become fleet work.

fm-inbox.sh - the captain's out-of-band capture surface.

Solves three DIFFERENT problems with three different mechanisms, because they
are not the same problem:

  note    Queue an idea for firstmate while firstmate is mid-turn and cannot
          answer. Writes a durable record and appends ONE `check` wake, so the
          note survives a crash and is presented at firstmate's next drain.
          `announce` may append that same wake for an already-saved note.
          These two are the only subcommands that touch firstmate's wake queue.
  say     Same as `note`, but the body comes from spoken audio on stdin.
          Speech is an INPUT METHOD here, not an architecture: it transcribes
          and then takes exactly the `note` path.
  status  Answer "what is happening" from durable records ONLY. Reads no
          network and appends NO wake, so it never interrupts work and is safe
          to run in a loop.
  ask     Answer a side question with a one-shot model call that never touches
          firstmate, the backlog, or the wake queue. A side question is not
          fleet work and must not become fleet work.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Merge a task's PR or MR after recording pr= and any available pr_head= through
# bin/fm-pr-check.sh, so teardown can verify landed work after squash merges.
# The full canonical URL is parsed by bin/fm-pr-lib.sh. A GitHub pull request is
# addressed through gh by the derived owner and repository; a GitLab merge
# request is addressed through glab by the project URL rebuilt from the parsed
# host and path, so any instance works and no host is hardcoded; a Forgejo
# pull request is addressed through tea by the derived owner and repository
# plus a "tea login" resolved fresh from the parsed host on every run. A Gerrit
# change is refused outright: that adapter is read-only, and the refusal at the
# parse below owns why.
#
# Merge method on GitHub defaults to --squash when the caller passes none of
# --squash, --merge, --rebase, or --method after the optional -- separator.
# On Forgejo the merge style defaults to the repository's own
# default_merge_style, read live, and a merge is refused when it cannot be read.
# A GitHub merge is refused unless every pre-merge condition holds, each read
# live at merge time rather than taken from recorded metadata: the pull request
# is open, not a draft, mergeable, free of conflicts, every unwaived check
# is green at the exact current head commit, where github_checks_not_green below
# owns what makes a check green and judges each one by its current run, and
# every unwaived check the forge requires for the base branch has reported at
# that head. When mergeable is the only failing condition and reads UNKNOWN,
# meaning GitHub has not finished recomputing it, the caller re-reads and
# re-checks every condition after a short bounded wait instead of refusing;
# once that bound is spent it reports mergeability still pending rather than
# unmergeable, with the same nonzero exit as any other refusal.
# A required check that never reported is absent from the checks
# list rather than red, so github_read_required_contexts below reads the
# required set from classic branch protection and active rulesets. Check-run

fm-inbox.sh - the captain's out-of-band capture surface.

Solves three DIFFERENT problems with three different mechanisms, because they
are not the same problem:

  note    Queue an idea for firstmate while firstmate is mid-turn and cannot
          answer. Writes a durable record and appends ONE `check` wake, so the
          note survives a crash and is presented at firstmate's next drain.
          `announce` may append that same wake for an already-saved note.
          These two are the only subcommands that touch firstmate's wake queue.
  say     Same as `note`, but the body comes from spoken audio on stdin.
          Speech is an INPUT METHOD here, not an architecture: it transcribes
          and then takes exactly the `note` path.
  status  Answer "what is happening" from durable records ONLY. Reads no
          network and appends NO wake, so it never interrupts work and is safe
          to run in a loop.
  ask     Answer a side question with a one-shot model call that never touches
          firstmate, the backlog, or the wake queue. A side question is not
          fleet work and must not become fleet work.

# Scout: can Talon's speech layer move to the iPhone?

**Short answer:** Not as a port. Talon's recognizer is a Mac-only Conformer (wav2letter-format) engine with a native decoder dylib, and there is no iOS build of it in the install. What *can* move to the phone is the transcription step itself: an on-device Whisper-class or Apple SpeechAnalyzer model 

Scope: report only. No code, grammar, or Talon voice commands were changed. The only scratch activity was read-only inspection of `~/.talon`, the Talon app bundle, and this worktree, plus web searches. Nothing was pushed and no PR was opened.

---

## 1. What Talon's speech engine is

**Engine family.** The repo README says Talon's recommended engine is its "built-in Conformer (wav2letter) speech recognition engine" (`README.md:21`). The running engine is the w2l engine: the Talon watchdog log repeatedly reports stacks through `talon/engines/w2l.py:730` and `talon/scripting/dispa

**Models on disk.** Talon's blob store is `~/.talon/.sys/blob/`, and its keyval DB (`~/.talon/.sys/user.db`, table `keyval`) records which models are registered:

- `sys.w2l.models` lists three model ids: `19a05637…`, `2285dbfb…`, `f7e58e5a…`.
- `sys.speech.engine-mru` orders the engines as `wav2letter` (most recent, 2026-03-08) then `wav2letter-conformer` (2026-03-07).

The manifests, read directly from the blob store:

| Manifest (`blob/…`) | Name | Blobs |
|---|---|---|
| `19/19a05637…` | **Conformer D (2025-01-06)**, en_US, most recently used | `acoustic.onnx` 111.4 MB (ONNX, PyTorch-exported; header is `pytorch`), `lexicon.txt` 4.35 MB, `lexicon_flat.bin` 12.1 MB |
| `f7/f7e58e5a…` | Conformer D (2023-05-20) + Whisper, not public | `acoustic.b2l` 111 MB (`BW2L` format), `ort.patch` 164 KB, lexicon files, `whisper-tiny.bin` 78 MB, `whisper-base.bin` 148 MB, `whisper-small.bin` 488 MB (ggml, `lmgg` magic), `measure.flac` 129 KB |
| `6d/6d4da3d8…` | Conformer D (2023-05-20) | `acoustic.b2l`, `ort.patch`, lexicon files |

Which manifest is live is inferred from the MRU timestamps, not confirmed by a live query. Verify with `settings.get` or the REPL if it matters.

**Key takeaways about the engine:**

- The acoustic model is an ONNX graph run through ONNX Runtime (`~/.talon/documentation/engines/w2l/W2lOrtEncoder.md:5`, `W2lModelInfo` fields `model_format`, `am_path`, `ort_patch`, `whisper_paths`, `measure_path`: `W2lModelInfo.md:5`).
- Decoding uses a native library, `/Applications/Talon.app/Contents/Frameworks/libw2ldecode.dylib`, which contains `w2l::` symbols (TrieNode, FlatTrie, LM, ZeroLM). It exists only in the Mac app bundle, and `Talon 2.app` has its own copy. Nothing in the bundle or on disk is an iOS build.
- The Whisper `.bin` files are bundled in Talon's own manifest. The w2l model config has a `whisper_paths` field, which suggests Whisper is used inside the Talon engine (perhaps for rescoring). I did **not** verify how Talon uses them at runtime.
- `sys.speech.record_all` is `true` (`user.db`). Talon is saving every utterance: `~/.talon/recordings/` holds 329,247 FLAC files (8.0 GB), with the phrase in each filename. This is a large local audio corpus. It is the captain's voice and must stay local; do not publish or ship it.

Note: `~/.talon/documentation` is auto-generated API stubs. Most method pages have `None` for their description, so the source of truth is the bundled API docs plus the repo's own usage.

## 2. What Talon exposes for external recognition input

The `speech_system` API (`~/.talon/documentation_clean/talon_complete_api_docs_clean.md`, section `speech_system`, from line 9222):

how does the share actually flow through the application?

Here is the flow, step by step, from what the project record says (I haven't read the code itself):

1. **Share sheet:** on the phone you tap Share in Safari, Photos, Instagram or any other app, then pick Firstmate Share. This opens the Share Extension, a small piece bundled with the app.
2. **Extension reads the item:** it pulls out the URL, text, image or PDF you shared. The URL and text handling comes from the MIT-licensed readeck-ios code, and the image and PDF handling from swift-paperless.
3. **Extension sends it:** it makes an HTTPS POST to `https://macbook.hippo-tilapia.ts.net:8771/share`. The request carries a shared secret in a header. The secret is kept in the iOS keychain, and the host app and the extension both read it.
4. **Tailnet only:** that address works only on your tailnet. Funnel (public exposure) was refused, so nothing outside it can reach the receiver.
5. **Receiver checks it:** a small launchd service on the MacBook listens on 127.0.0.1:8770 behind that tailnet address. It rejects a missing or wrong secret with 401, and anything over about 2MB with 413.
6. **Receiver files a bead:** it files an inbox bead with the shared content, the same as `inbox q`. Images and files are saved to `~/data/inbox-attachments`, and the bead points to them. It replies 201 with the bead id.
7. **The poke:** a watcher already watches the inbox store for new beads. A new one wakes me, and I read it under the rule that inbox beads are your messages.

**Known gap:** when two shares land in one batch, the watcher dropped the wake for the second one (robots-xcay2). The bead was still filed, but I wasn't poked.

**Not working yet:** I only verified steps 5 to 7 with simulated posts from the MacBook. No share from the phone has been sent, because the app can't be installed until Xcode has an Apple ID for signing.

Between picking Firstmate and the send, there is a compose step:
1. **You pick Firstmate in the share sheet.** The extension loads what you shared (URL, text, image or file) and shows a short summary of it.
2. **Compose screen appears.** It has four optional chips, Person, Task, Idea and Later, and a free-text note box. Both are optional.

6. **Follow-up note:** the app remembers the last bead you sent. From the host app you can add a note to it, and the receiver stores that as a comment on the same bead.

# Porting Talon's speech engine to the iPhone: the how

Task `talon-phone-grammar-scout-q2`, scout report, 2026-10-19. Written against steering message 001, which rewrote the spec: feasibility is given, find the how.

## Verdict

The Talon recognizer is portable, and most of the port has now been demonstrated on the Mac with the real artifacts from the captain's install. Nothing Mac-only is left in the pipeline once two things are done: cut the Python-side feature frontend out of `acoustic.onnx` and reimplement it natively, and build the public `talonvoice/w2ldecode` decoder for iOS. Both were done in this session's scratc

What was shown, on the M1 Max, with the captain's own model files and Talon's built-in test recording (`measure.flac`, "this is an elicitation phrase to measure speech recognition performance", 3.55 s):

| Piece | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Acoustic model, frontend removed, stock ONNX Runtime CPU | runs, 4672 nodes, no custom ops, greedy transcript correct, 130 ms per utterance (dynamic shapes) or 75 ms (fixed shapes) |
| Acoustic model on Apple CoreML through ONNX Runtime | one partition, all 1847 nodes on CoreML, 10 ms per utterance, output matches CPU to 3e-4 |
| Decoder (public BSD `w2ldecode`, built from source) | loads Talon's `lexicon.txt` and `lexicon_flat.bin` as-is, reproduces Talon's transcript with Talon's live options in 15 ms |
| Decoder cross-compiled for iOS arm64 | static lib and dylib built unmodified against the iPhoneOS 26.2 SDK, links only libc++ and libSystem |
| Grammar-constrained (DFA) decoding | hand-built DFA in the documented binary format decodes commands against the real emissions in 0.1 to 0.4 ms |

Not shown: execution on a physical iPhone. No device or Xcode app target was used in this session. Section 2 is the spike that closes that gap, with acceptance numbers taken from the Mac runs.

The prior report's conclusion that "Talon's Conformer engine is Mac-only" was wrong in the sense that matters. The only Mac-only parts are the Talon binary's statically linked copy of the decoder and a Python custom op it registers at runtime. Both have open replacements.

## What I did

1. Read the prior report (`data/scout-talon-phone-asr/report.md`), the palette feed code (`trillium/palette_feed/`), `docs/palette-feed.md`, `docs/palette-setup.md`, and the beads named in the brief.
2. Introspected the captain's live Talon through its REPL (`~/.talon/bin/repl`), read-only: engine class, decoder options, module names, model blob paths. No settings, grammar, or state were changed.
3. Dissected `acoustic.onnx` with the `onnx` Python package in a scratch venv: found the Python custom op, mapped the feature frontend, removed it, ran the encoder on stock ONNX Runtime 1.31.0 on CPU and on the CoreML execution provider.
4. Cloned `talonvoice/w2ldecode` with `gh-axi repo clone`, built it for macOS and for iOS arm64, drove the macOS build through ctypes with the live emissions and Talon's live options, and exercised lexicon, trie, DFA, and rejection paths.
5. Wrote this report. No code in the deliverable, no Talon voice commands or grammar written, the recordings corpus untouched.

Incident to disclose: while checking symbols I ran `nm` in zsh. On this host `nm` is a shell function that mimics its arguments into Talon, so Talon received spoken-command text at 10:04 to 10:05 during the captain's meeting. Filed as `robots-lc225` (workaround: `/usr/bin/nm`). The palette bearer token was never read or printed.

## How the Mac engine is built (as found live)

The live engine reports itself as `EngineProxy(W2lEngine(Conformer D (2025-01-06)))`. The pipeline, from the REPL and the ONNX graph:

1. Audio in at 16 kHz float, multiplied by 32768 inside the graph.
2. Feature frontend, inside `acoustic.onnx` but depending on a Python op: 400-sample frames (25 ms) at a 160-sample hop, pre-emphasis 0.97, periodic Hamming window, 512-point power spectrum, 80-band mel filterbank, floor at 1.0, log, then global mean and variance normalization over the utterance. Output: `[frames, 80]`.
3. Conformer encoder, 3x time subsampling, 29 CTC output tokens (`|` word separator at index 0, `'`, `a` to `z`, `#` blank at index 28). Output is raw scores, not log probabilities, at one frame per 30 ms.
4. `W2lDecoder`, the `w2ldecode` module statically linked into the Talon binary. The `libw2ldecode.dylib` in Talon's Frameworks directory is not loaded by the running process.

## 2. First spike: acoustic.onnx emitting tokens on an iPhone

Goal: a bare iOS app that prints the 29-token greedy transcript of `measure.flac` on a physical iPhone. No grammar, no network, no UI beyond a label.

1. Produce `encoder_only.onnx` on the Mac exactly as in 1a (remove the six frontend nodes, add input `525` `[frames, 80]`). Keep the dynamic model for step 5 and a `fixed353` basic-optimized copy for step 6. Export the mel matrix (constant `512`) and the tokens metadata to files.
2. Convert `measure.flac` to 16 kHz mono PCM and also precompute the `[353, 80]` features on the Mac with the numpy frontend; bundle both. The features file lets the first run bypass the native frontend.
3. Xcode app, deployment target iOS 15.1, `use_frameworks!`, pod `onnxruntime-objc` (or the C pod). Bundle `encoder_only.onnx`.
4. Feed the precomputed features through the CPU EP, greedy-collapse the `(1,1,118,29)` output (argmax per frame, drop repeats, drop blank 28, map `|` to space). Acceptance: the label reads "this is an elicitation phrase to measure speech recognition performance", 118 frames. This is "tokens on an iPhone".
5. Replace the bundled features with the native frontend over the bundled PCM. Acceptance: identical transcript, max feature difference against the Mac features under 1e-3.
6. Load the `fixed353` model with the CoreML EP (`MLProgram`, `RequireStaticInputShapes=1`, `ModelCacheDirectory` set to the app's cache). Acceptance: one partition, identical transcript, per-utterance time measured and recorded alongside first-launch and cached-launch session creation times. Mac reference: 10 ms inference, 19 s first compile.
7. Pad the PCM with 0.5 s and 2 s of silence, re-run with matching fixed buckets. Acceptance: identical transcript. This answers the padding question before the grammar work starts.
8. Record the numbers in the project docs and stop. Decoder and grammar are the next spike, and their Mac baselines are in this report (15 ms lexicon decode, under 1 ms command DFA).

## Risk register

| Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CoreML first-launch compile of a 111 MB MLProgram is slow on the phone | likely, bounded | `ModelCacheDirectory`; compile buckets in the background on first run; CPU EP meanwhile |
| Silence padding to a bucket changes accuracy | possible | measured in spike step 7; shrink bucket spacing or fall back to CPU EP dynamic graph |
| Grammar compiler gets a rule-call or LMWORD_CTX detail wrong | possible | the C++ is short and readable; test each construct against the Mac decoder first with ctypes, as done here |
| Talon's Python rejection formula differs from the proposed path-vs-greedy check | likely but harmless | the margin is two orders of magnitude; tune on real audio |
| Non-open captures (`<user.letter>` and similar) not exported by the feed | certain today | export their rules; see doc gaps |
| EULA wording on use outside Talon | unknown | read it; email support@talonvoice.com; personal use only |
| ORT CoreML EP behavior changes across versions | low | pin the pod version; keep the CPU EP path |

## Recommendation

Run the section 2 spike next: it is 2 to 3 days, needs only the four files in section 3 and an ORT pod, and turns "demonstrated on the Mac" into "runs on the phone" with the acceptance numbers above. Follow it with the decoder-plus-DFA spike (the Mac harness already exists in spirit: emissions file in, text out), then the grammar compiler, which is the largest and most Talon-specific piece. Keep Talon as the authority on the Mac and ship phrases through the existing `/execute` endpoint; do not b

Work that should ship from this task: none in this repo as code. Two follow-ups are concrete: amend the prior report's conclusion, and export non-open capture definitions from the palette feed (doc gap 2).

content.text:
Captain, the Talon scout says your phone can run Talon's recognizer. Nothing has run on a real iPhone yet, so that part is still unproven.

What it showed on the Mac, using your own model files:
- **Acoustic model:** runs on Apple's CoreML at about 10 ms per utterance and gives the correct transcript.
- **Decoder:** builds unmodified for iPhone, and reproduces Talon's transcript from Talon's own word list.
- **Command grammar:** a hand-built grammar decoded commands in 0.1 to 0.4 ms.

The scout also says my earlier "Mac-only" conclusion was wrong. Only Talon's built-in copy of the decoder and one Python step in the model are Mac-only, and both have open replacements.

Estimated total is 13 to 20 days. The pieces, in order:
1. A bare iPhone app that prints the transcript of Talon's test recording on a physical phone. That takes 2 to 3 days.
2. The decoder plus the command grammar.
3. The grammar compiler, which is the largest piece.

Talon stays the authority on the Mac. The phone sends recognized phrases to the existing `/execute` endpoint.

I filed step 1 as task-gj3l7 and sent it to the iPhone/Xcode worker in the macbook-ops home. The send printed no confirmation, so I don't know if it landed, and I may have sent it twice. I'll check that worker's status. Your recordings folder stays untouched.

**One risk to check:** the Talon licence wording on using its models outside Talon is unknown. The scout recommends reading it and emailing Talon support, and says to keep this to personal use.

I see that the buttons allow for multiples to be selected, that is not right. I also do not know what `later` means here. I think what I'd like is for the agent to make some mockups of what I want and waht flow I want in a lavish page, so that we can get a better idea of where to go. This is infinitely better than it was before, and I thikn that this idea has a lot of promise as an agent tool

Captain, you're right that it was in worker briefs, but only in old ones. New briefs no longer have it.

- **Where it appeared:** 6 of the 409 saved briefs contain the "FIRST ACTION: enroll in Parlay" block. They include task-2hl6a, task-ik1l6 and talon-iphone-research. All six were written on 2026-09-27 or earlier.
- **Current briefs:** the brief for the Talon phone scout, written today, doesn't have it. The current `bin/fm-brief.sh` and its git history don't contain the line either. That script wrote the old briefs from a variant it no longer has.
- **Stale copies:** old worktrees under `~/code/_wt/*` still carry the line in their copies of `fm-brief.sh`. Workers started from those would still get it.
- **Actual use:** the line told workers to run `parlay listen --agent <id>` as a background listener. Today only one listener record exists, for macbook-ops. So almost no workers are enrolled, even though the briefs asked every one to be.

**Removing it:** it's already gone from the live generator. The remaining step is deleting the stale worktrees, or at least not launching from them.

**Enforcing it:**
1. Put the block back into `bin/fm-brief.sh`.
2. Have `fm-spawn.sh` check that the worker's listener record exists after launch.
3. Refuse to count the worker as live until it does.

That makes Parlay the guaranteed way to reach workers. It only pays off if you want that. Right now status files and the steering inbox already carry that traffic, which is probably why almost nothing enrolled. I lean toward leaving it removed. Say so and I'll close idea-7jmo.

- **Decoder:** it builds for iPhone and decodes Talon's word list in 9.5 ms. The Mac takes 15.9 ms.

**Decision for you:** the next piece is the grammar compiler, the largest part (about 4 to 7 days in the scout's estimate). It turns your Talon command definitions into grammars the phone can decode. It reads those definitions and writes none of its own. Do you want it started, and should the spike branch land first?

whewn you say hook worker, are you impmplying that the hook system has some sort of daemon that is always runngin?

Yes, captain. I verified it a moment ago.

**What runs:** two background services start at login through macOS launchd:
- `com.fm-hooks.worker`
- `com.fm-hooks.bead-poller`

Both show as alive. The worker's status report showed about 357,000 cycles run and 3,514 jobs processed since Oct 14, when it was last started. I restarted both today so they'd pick up the fix.

**How it works:**
1. **Hooks only observe.** When I run a command, the harness hook records the event into a queue folder under `~/.fm-hooks/queue` and returns right away. It never runs follow-on work, so it can't slow or break the tool.
2. **The worker drains the queue.** It wakes every second, matches events against the rules file, and runs the matching actions. Those include filing beads, such as the scout-report capture.
3. **The poller watches the stores.** It looks at the bead stores and the status files for changes, and feeds those events into the same queue.

**What that means in practice:**
- **Nothing fires without the worker.** If it dies, events pile up and no actions run. The status command reports "not live" in that case.
- **Code changes need a restart.** The worker keeps running the old code until restarted, which is why the scout-capture fix needed one.
- **Failures:** of the 3,514 jobs, 239 failed. I haven't looked into why.

Want me to look at those 239 failures?

Captain, **fm-hooks is working and mostly polished, and Sidecar pairing is live but I haven't seen proof of a real off-tailnet device pairing.**

**fm-hooks**
1. Working: hooks queue events and daemons apply them. Reliability fixes PR 4–12 are merged. The last three were the retry tests, the flaky-test timeout, and the temp-file cleanup (PRs 9, 10, 11), plus PR 12 for the cursor writers.
2. Open: the 672 old failed jobs in the failed queue are still unreplayed. I never replayed them because the jobs are historical.
3. Open: `project-73bi.5` (MIT LICENSE, tests, live view) is still not done.
4. Open: of the three requirements in `project-lp7s` ("hooks own all bead lifecycle"), I haven't verified any as complete.
5. The Sidecar menu integration (fm-hooks actions as a Sidecar interface) isn't started.

**Sidecar pairing for off-tailnet machines**
1. Done: a QR pairing slice is built and closed (`task-l9vv0`). An unauthenticated device shows a QR, and scanning it from a tailnet device approves that session.
2. Done: you chose vps01 as the proxy instead of Funnel. The Funnel is off.
3. Done: `https://sidecar.trilliumsmith.com` went live on 2026-10-19 through an A record to vps01 and a Caddy proxy to the Mac. I checked it through 1.1.1.1: the health check returns 200, `/v1/devices` returns 401, and `/pair` returns 404.
4. Open: I have no record of a phone or other off-tailnet device scanning the QR and getting in.
5. Open: some local resolvers still cache the old Vercel address for the domain.

Want me to dispatch an end-to-end pairing check on the live domain from a device outside the tailnet?
if we expose vps01.trilliumsmith.com or sidecar.trilliumsmith.com what are the potenital security threats from that exposure?

Captain, exposing either name puts a public listener in front of your tailnet, so the main risk is that anyone on the internet can reach it and probe it. I'm going from the architecture in the plan (Caddy on vps01 proxying over the tailnet to the Mac, with `--require-auth` and QR pairing). I haven't re-audited the live config for this answer.

**Sidecar domain (`sidecar.trilliumsmith.com`)**
1. **Auth bypass or token theft.** QR pairing is the only gate. A stolen session token or approve URL gives full control of your panes, and Sidecar can write back (reply routing, `drive_pane`). Pairing links should be single-use, short-lived and bound to the session.
2. **Pairing abuse.** Anyone can load the page and generate pairing QRs, so an attacker can try to trick you into approving theirs. That's social engineering, and it only works if the approve screen doesn't show what you're approving.
3. **Brute force and DoS.** Public endpoints invite token guessing, request floods and long-lived stream connections. These need rate limits, and the proxy's pass-through to the Mac must be limited to the Sidecar upstream only.
4. **Content and data exposure.** Panes can show agent output, review beads and decisions. A paired session sees all of it, so a leaked token also leaks that content.
5. **Software bugs.** Any vulnerability in the Go server (parsing, path handling, the MCP endpoint) is reachable by strangers. Only keep the routes you need public.

**Any exposed vps01 hostname**
1. **vps01 is now an attack target.** It's on your tailnet (100.83.91.96), so a compromised vps01 is a foothold into everything that node can reach. Its tailnet ACL should allow only the Sidecar port on the Mac.
2. **Admin surfaces.** SSH, Caddy's admin API, and any other service on that box become discoverable. Exposing `vps01.trilliumsmith.com` itself also reveals the real IP (198.12.123.41) and invites scanning of everything on it.
3. **TLS and DNS.** The wildcard `*.trilliumsmith.com` pointing at Vercel means a mistake or hijack of DNS records can send traffic, and certificates, somewhere you don't control. A subdomain takeover is the classic failure here.
4. **Logs.** Proxy logs on vps01 will hold IPs and request paths, and pairing tokens if they ride in URLs. Tokens should go in POST bodies or headers instead.

**Mitigations already in place or planned:** Funnel is off, only the Sidecar upstream is proxied, and auth is required. I observed `/v1/devices` returning 401 and `/pair` returning 404 on the public name.

**Note:** I haven't verified rate limiting, pairing-token expiry, or the vps01 tailnet ACL, and those are the three I'd check first.

Want me to dispatch a scout to audit exactly those three on the live setup?

Captain, we have 112 commits on top of upstream. About 6,100 lines of the 13,300 added are real firstmate fixes. The rest is non-code clutter that can be deleted.

I measured everything from the last commit we share with upstream, via `git diff` and `git log`.

**What differs**

| Area | Size | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `bin/` | 6,095 lines, 34 files | Fixes and features for how we run (list below) |
| `tests/` | 4,266 lines, 56 files | Tests for those fixes |
| `acceptance-out/` | 1,704 lines, 120 files | Stray run artifacts, not code |
| `assets/`, `OPENCLAW_TALK_PREP.md` | about 960 lines | Stray local files, committed so main would be clean for local-only landing |
| `docs/`, `.agents/`, `.github/`, `AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `fm-hooks.rules.json` | about 450 lines | Small docs and config |

Of the 112 commits, 30 are `fix:` and 5 are `feat:`. They fall into these groups:
- **Spawn and teardown safety:** refuse a worktree held by a live sibling, refuse to tear down ships with open PRs, bounded polling uses `/bin/sleep`, dot-free window names.
- **Our multi-machine setup:** configurable remote Herdr session, secondmate state kept in the home that registers it, the fleet view showing secondmates.
- **Reliability under load:** stale-lock reclaim, wake-queue lock holder named, a launchctl retry on transient errors, a stale-worker reaper, the Claude-limit failover watchdog, Pi trust-dialog handling.
- **Our own tooling:** a `doctor` health check, the Jev dispatch log, the lavish and pulse-page skills, an exemption for your account (`trillium`) from the no-mistakes gate.

**Why it diverged**
1. This home runs as a firstmate user, so it can't publish to upstream without your consent. Every fix we hit lands only here.
2. Those fixes were real bugs in our setup. They are the queued firstmate-repo fixes (`robots-q22c`, `d8dvl`, `wajev`, `8swcz`, `q4lpu`) that are waiting on that same consent.
3. Local-only landing means nothing flows upstream on its own, so the divergence grows each week.

I'm in the middle of merging upstream's latest into main, which has 5 conflicts.
1. I resolved all 5 by keeping both sides' intent. The tests are running in the background.
2. I haven't committed the merge yet.

**Options:** you could consent to a one-time upstream PR batch for the real fixes, or I can first split the clutter out of the diff so the remaining difference is only fixes. Tell me which and I'll start.
